opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think symmetry is one of the most fundamental ideas in all of science, and it's been somewhat underappreciated in machine learning until fairly recently. If you look at physics, a huge part of its progress in the twentieth century came from recognizing symmetries. Noether's theorem tells you that every conservation law corresponds to a symmetry, and the Standard Model is essentially built on gauge symmetries. So if symmetry is that central to how the world works, it would be very surprising if it weren't central to learning about the world.

From a machine learning point of view, the reason symmetries matter is that they're one of the most powerful forms of inductive bias you can have. Learning is impossible without assumptions; that's the no-free-lunch theorem. The question is always which assumptions are the right ones. Symmetries are a beautiful answer, because they let you take what you learned in one situation and transfer it to all the situations related by the symmetry transformation. Convolutional neural networks are the canonical example: translation invariance means that if you learn to recognize a cat in one corner of the image, you can recognize it anywhere. That one idea is a big part of why convnets worked so well. Geometric deep learning generalizes it, saying let's do the same thing for rotations, permutations, graphs, manifolds, gauge transformations, and so on, and gives you a unified framework for all of that.

This is something I've been interested in for a long time. Years ago, Robert Gens and I worked on deep symmetry networks, which generalized convnets to arbitrary symmetry groups. So it's very gratifying to see the field come around to this.

Having said that, I'd add a caveat, which is that I don't think it's the whole story. The symmetries in geometric deep learning are mostly exact, known in advance, and fairly low-level: things like rotations and translations. But a lot of the symmetries in the real world are approximate, or they're higher-level and abstract, and we don't know them ahead of time. The really exciting frontier is learning the symmetries from data rather than hard-coding them. If you can discover the symmetries of a domain, you've in a sense discovered a big part of its structure. And of course, symmetry has to be combined with other things, like compositionality and logical structure, to get to really general intelligence. But as one of the pieces of the puzzle, I think it's a very important one, and it's great that people are taking it seriously.

r002.rationale: It describes symmetries as powerful inductive biases, but does not say that weak inductive biases enabling successful machine learning are fundamentally symmetries.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the reason I'm enthusiastic is that symmetries are really the right language for talking about what deep learning has been doing all along, without quite admitting it. If you look at why convolutional networks worked so spectacularly well, it's not some mysterious property of depth. It's that they bake in translation invariance. An object is the same object whether it's in the upper left or lower right of the image, and instead of making the network learn that from millions of examples, you just build it in. That's an enormous amount of knowledge you're giving the learner for free, and it's knowledge you're completely certain is correct.

What geometric deep learning does is say, okay, that was one symmetry. What about rotations, what about permutations, what about the symmetries of a graph, of a molecule, of a manifold? And it turns out there's this beautiful body of mathematics, group theory and representation theory, that tells you exactly how to construct architectures that respect those symmetries. So it takes something that was a clever engineering trick and turns it into a principle. I've always argued that the way you make learning work is by having the right assumptions, and symmetries are among the purest assumptions you can make. They don't say what the function is, they say what it can't depend on, and that shrinks the hypothesis space enormously while being almost always true for physical problems.

The other thing I'd say, and this is closer to my own heart, is that this is a case where the deep learning community is rediscovering something that logicians and old-school AI people knew, which is that structure matters. Symmetry is a form of prior knowledge, and you're encoding it in the architecture rather than in rules. I think the next step, and this is where it gets interesting, is to realize that the symmetries we care about aren't only geometric. There are symmetries in reasoning, in language, in programs. Once you see that, the question becomes whether we can learn the symmetries themselves rather than hand-specifying them, and that's where I think the real action is going to be.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that symmetry gives us a principled way to build prior knowledge into learning. If I move an object across an image, it’s still the same object. A learner shouldn’t have to discover that from thousands of examples. We can build that constraint into the architecture, and then use the data to learn what we don’t already know.

Convolutional networks are a very successful example of this idea. Geometric deep learning asks how we can extend it to other transformations and other kinds of structure, like graphs. That’s appealing because it turns a collection of architectural tricks into something more systematic: identify the transformations that should preserve the answer, or transform it in a predictable way, and design the learner accordingly.

The interesting question, of course, is which symmetries actually hold in your problem. Get those right, and you can make learning much more efficient. Get them wrong, and you’ve built the wrong assumption into the model.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that symmetry gives us a very powerful way to put knowledge about the world into a learning algorithm. If I move an object across an image, it’s still the same object. The learner shouldn’t have to discover that from scratch by seeing it in every possible position. Convolutional networks exploit that idea, and geometric deep learning extends it to richer transformations and structures, like graphs.

That matters because learning is fundamentally about generalization. What lets you go from the examples you’ve seen to examples you haven’t? Symmetries tell you that certain changes should preserve the answer, or change it in a predictable way. Build that into the architecture, and you can potentially learn with much less data.

The interesting question, of course, is which symmetries to build in. You want the right assumptions for the problem. But as a principle for designing learning systems, I think it’s tremendously fruitful.
